title: Sri Chand the ascetic
hook: Nanak's elder son chose a celibate life; the Udasi order traces itself to him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Sulakhni, and your line, the one who stayed. Did your thanks reach the person who kept home going? Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

A family business, three generations in. The father built it. Everyone assumes the eldest will take the keys. But the eldest's heart is somewhere else, and in the end the keys go to someone outside the family. Nobody is disowned. Families know this scene. Guru Nanak's family knew it too. Yesterday we met Mata Sulakhni and her two sons. Today we follow the elder one, Sri Chand, who chose a life his father didn't choose. Today's word: Udasi.
screen: `THE ELDEST SAYS NO.` → `A ROAD OF HIS OWN.` → `TODAY: SRI CHAND.`

segments.voice: Sri Chand grew up while his father was out on the long road. And he grew into a man drawn to stillness and renunciation. Tradition remembers him as an ascetic: celibate, living apart from the household, devoted to meditation. He never married. And the Udasis, an order of renunciants, trace themselves to him. Udasi is a word Sikhs already know from Nanak's own life, because the Guru's great journeys are called his udasis. So the son's order carries a name that echoes the father's travels. Here's the tension, and the tellings don't hide it. Guru Nanak's own way, as his hymns describe it, was the householder's way: earn honestly, share, remember God in the middle of family and work. He came home to Kartarpur, to the fields and the family. And when it came time to choose who would carry the light after him, he didn't choose either son. He chose Lehna, and named him Angad. Sri Chand went another way. So what do the stories know? They hold two things at once. Sikh teaching follows the householder path the Gurus walked. And tradition still remembers Sri Chand with honor, as Baba Sri Chand, the Guru's son, a man of deep devotion who took a different road. Tradition remembers later Gurus and Sri Chand meeting with respect. Udasi teachers, tradition says, went on honoring Guru Nanak and singing his word. That is how respect for a different choice looks in a family of faith: you don't pretend the roads are the same, and you don't stop calling each other family.
screen: `A SON DRAWN TO STILLNESS.` · `UDASI, AN ECHO OF THE JOURNEYS.` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER'S PATH, AND ANOTHER.` · `REMEMBERED WITH HONOR.` · then, large: `A DIFFERENT PATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect a different choice. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind someone close who chose a road you didn't. A sibling who left the faith, or entered it more deeply. A child who took a different job, a different city, a different kind of life. A friend who stayed single, or married young. Notice the old argument that rises. Don't try to settle it. Just look at them, choosing, and find one thing in their choice you can honestly honor. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Udasi. The order of renunciants that traces itself to Baba Sri Chand, Guru Nanak's elder son, and a name that echoes the Guru's own journeys.
Your line: a different path. Today, tell that person one thing you respect about the road they chose, without adding a but. Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

notes: 'The later Gurus and Sri Chand are remembered meeting with respect': tradition tells of meetings with Guru Ram Das and others; confirm the phrasing is fair and not overstated.
'Udasi teachers, tradition says, went on honoring Guru Nanak and singing his word': confirm; later history of Udasi custodianship of shrines deliberately left out.
'The Guru's great journeys are called his udasis': confirm the usage. No etymology of 'udasi' is claimed.
'Sri Chand grew up while his father was out on the long road' follows the outline's framing; confirm.
Sensitive: the succession passing over both sons is stated plainly without blame; confirm a Keeper is comfortable with the tone.

Auditor: hook said the eldest 'says no' to the keys, which implied Sri Chand declined the succession; tradition says Guru Nanak passed over both sons for Lehna. Hook rewritten to match. 'Remembered meeting with respect' now marked 'tradition remembers'.
